## Data

The data are seasonally adjusted monthly unemployment rates for the United
States, Oregon, California, Texas, and New York. They come from the Federal
Reserve Economic Data (FRED) database and are identified by the series codes
UNRATE, ORUR, CAUR, TXUR, and NYUR. The series were requested starting in
January 1976. Because `tq_get()` may fail when accessing FRED, I use the
`unemp_raw.rds` dataset provided by Professor Piger and stored in the project's
`data` folder, following his October 16 instructions.

```{r}
#| label: load-packages
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
```

```{r}
#| label: read-data
#| echo: true
# Use the data file Professor Piger provided as an email attachment.
# It must be saved inside this project as data/unemp_raw.rds.
unemp_raw <- read_rds("data/unemp_raw.rds")
head(unemp_raw)
```

The saved observations cover `r format(min(unemp_raw$date), "%B %Y")` through
`r format(max(unemp_raw$date), "%B %Y")`. Each row represents a region in one
month. The `price` field in the original data contains the unemployment rate.

## Wrangling

First, I renamed the rate variable and mapped each FRED series code to a
readable region name. I then filled October 2025 with September 2025's value
within each region, as instructed, before computing monthly changes in
percentage points. I also created a sample starting in January 2015 and identified the largest monthly increases and decreases after excluding 2020.

```{r}
#| label: wrangle-data
#| echo: true
unemp <- unemp_raw |>
  rename(unemployment_rate = price) |>
  mutate(
    region = case_when(
      symbol == "UNRATE" ~ "United States",
      symbol == "ORUR"   ~ "Oregon",
      symbol == "CAUR"   ~ "California",
      symbol == "TXUR"   ~ "Texas",
      symbol == "NYUR"   ~ "New York"
    )
  )

# Represent any skipped month explicitly before filling October 2025.
unemp <- unemp |>
  group_by(region, symbol) |>
  complete(date = seq.Date(min(date), max(date), by = "month")) |>
  ungroup()

unemp <- unemp |>
  arrange(region, date) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(
    unemployment_rate = replace(
      unemployment_rate,
      date == as.Date("2025-10-01"),
      unemployment_rate[date == as.Date("2025-09-01")]
    )
  ) |>
  ungroup()

unemp <- unemp |>
  arrange(region, date) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  mutate(
    unemployment_rate_change = unemployment_rate - lag(unemployment_rate)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

unemp_recent <- unemp |>
  filter(date >= as.Date("2015-01-01"))

unemp_summary <- unemp |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate = mean(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_rate = min(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_rate = max(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

unemp_recent_summary <- unemp_recent |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarize(
    mean_rate = mean(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_rate = min(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_rate = max(unemployment_rate, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

unemp_top_increases <- unemp |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_max(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE)

unemp_top_decreases <- unemp |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_min(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE)

unemp_no_covid <- unemp |>
  filter(format(date, "%Y") != "2020")

unemp_top_increases_no_covid <- unemp_no_covid |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_max(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate_change, unemployment_rate)

unemp_top_decreases_no_covid <- unemp_no_covid |>
  filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)) |>
  slice_min(unemployment_rate_change, n = 5, with_ties = TRUE) |>
  select(region, date, unemployment_rate_change, unemployment_rate)
```

### Table 1. Full-sample unemployment rate summary

This table shows the mean, minimum, and maximum unemployment rates for each
region across all available months in the saved data.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(unemp_summary, digits = 2,
      caption = "Full-sample unemployment rates (percent)")
```

### Table 2. Unemployment rate summary since January 2015

This table uses only months from January 2015 onward.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(unemp_recent_summary, digits = 2,
      caption = "Unemployment rates since January 2015 (percent)")
```

### Table 3. Largest monthly increases excluding 2020

This table lists the five largest month-over-month unemployment rate increases
outside 2020, including any tied values. Changes are measured in percentage
points.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(unemp_top_increases_no_covid, digits = 2,
      caption = "Largest monthly increases, excluding 2020")
```

### Table 4. Largest monthly decreases excluding 2020

This table lists the five largest decreases outside 2020, including any ties.

```{r}
#| echo: false
kable(unemp_top_decreases_no_covid, digits = 2,
      caption = "Largest monthly decreases, excluding 2020")
```

## Visualization

### Figure 1. Unemployment rates over time

The first chart puts the United States and four states on the same axes so their
unemployment-rate levels and common turning points can be compared.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
plot_5_1 <- ggplot(unemp, aes(x = date, y = unemployment_rate,
                             color = region)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55, na.rm = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly unemployment rates: U.S. and four states",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Unemployment rate (%)",
    color = "Region"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
plot_5_1
```

### Figure 2. Unemployment rates in individual panels

Faceting the same monthly series makes it easier to trace each region's pattern
without overlapping lines.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
plot_5_2 <- ggplot(unemp, aes(x = date, y = unemployment_rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue4", linewidth = 0.55, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ region) +
  labs(
    title = "Monthly unemployment rates by region",
    x = "Date",
    y = "Unemployment rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
plot_5_2
```

### Figure 3. Mean unemployment rates by region

The bars are ordered from the lowest to the highest full-sample average.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot_5_3 <- ggplot(
  unemp_summary,
  aes(x = fct_reorder(region, mean_rate), y = mean_rate)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue4") +
  labs(
    title = "Average unemployment rate by region, full sample",
    x = "Region (lowest to highest average)",
    y = "Mean unemployment rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
plot_5_3
```

### Figure 4. Size of monthly changes by region

For my additional plot, I compare the *absolute* month-to-month change in the
unemployment rate across regions using boxplots. I chose this because the line
plots show rate levels, while a distribution of monthly changes makes it easier
to compare how much the unemployment rate typically moves from month to month.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
plot_5_4 <- ggplot(
  unemp |> filter(!is.na(unemployment_rate_change)),
  aes(x = region, y = abs(unemployment_rate_change))
) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue3", outlier.alpha = 0.45) +
  labs(
    title = "Magnitude of monthly unemployment changes by region",
    x = "Region",
    y = "Absolute month-over-month change (percentage points)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1))
plot_5_4
```

## Reflection

This assignment helped me get more comfortable using R to work with data. Using the provided data file  made it easier to focus on organizing the data and creating the tables and graphs. One thing I had to pay more attention to was making sure the dates were in the right order when calculating monthly changes. I also thought it was interesting to see how excluding 2020 affected the results. Overall, I have a better understanding of how RStudio, Quarto, and GitHub work together.
